title: Lycra sheet model for teaching space-time curvature
description: A large stretched lycra sheet with golf balls is used to show how mass produces curvature in the fabric of the sheet, serving as "a 2-dimensional analogy for space-time." Using this model, students observe that curvature increases with mass, learn about circular and elliptical orbits, three-body interaction, and can test the inverse square law of gravitation. Toy cars with fixed steering represent light beams deflected in curved space, compared with images of gravitational lensing from the Hubble space telescope.
requirements: When using models it is important to point out their limitations
constraints: In the lycra sheet model, the apparent gravitational forces are created through components of the gravitational force acting on each ball, and the warping of time, essential to understanding gravity on Earth, is missing
target_learning_goals: understand that matter tells space-time how to curve and space-time tells matter how to move

article_title: Teaching Einsteinian Physics at Schools: Part 1, Models and Analogies for Relativity
citation: Kaur, T., Blair, D., Moschilla, J., Stannard, W. & Zadnik, M. (2017). Teaching Einsteinian Physics at Schools: Part 1, Models and Analogies for Relativity. The University of Western Australia. http://www.physics.uwa.edu.au
title: Space-time simulator: lycra membrane model for curved space and orbital motion
description: A physical model in which a lycra (spandex) membrane stretched across an elevated wooden frame represents deformable space; masses placed on it create curvature and simulate gravitational motion of balls and toy cars. The authors note it "has been used since 2002" and was independently developed at the University of Western Australia in 2005. Wu et al. are reported to have shown it "accurately represents planetary orbits, but breaks down for more complicated orbital systems, for instance equal mass binary systems."
requirements: Lycra membrane (1.2m x 1.2m), wooden frame (3m x 3m or 20 tent poles in a ring), 100 golf balls, ball bearings, spring-loaded toy cars with fixed steering
constraints: All gravitational effects in the model are created by Newtonian gravity; membrane friction limits binary-orbit demonstrations; edges repel balls; only a few precessing orbits are observable before the orbit deteriorates
target_learning_goals: understanding mass-curvature relationships, orbital motion, photon trajectories and gravitational lensing
examples: Students measure deformation versus mass, observe universality of free fall with pairs of balls of different masses, and derive the membrane force law from spring-balance measurements
key_sources: Kaur, T., Blair, D., Moschilla, J., Stannard, W. & Zadnik, M. (2017). Teaching Einsteinian Physics at Schools: Part 1, Models and Analogies for Relativity. The University of Western Australia. https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.02058
